context: Elementary number theory: congruence of integers modulo a fixed positive integer

formulations.mathematical_rationale: The source explicitly quantifies integer a,b and positive m; defining congruence by an integer multiple avoids ambiguous real or zero modulus conventions.
formulations.text: For m∈ℤ with m>0 and a,b∈ℤ, define a≡b (mod m) if and only if there exists k∈ℤ such that a−b=km. The modulus m is fixed and strictly positive.

formulations.mathematical_rationale: The remainder characterization is equivalent to integer-multiple congruence by Euclidean division with the same strictly positive integer modulus; no zero-modulus case is asserted.
formulations.text: Let m be a positive integer. For a,b∈ℤ write a≡b (mod m) precisely when the least nonnegative remainders of a and b upon division by m coincide.

context: Finite-dimensional linear algebra: n-by-n square matrices over a field K, n≥1

formulations.mathematical_rationale: The source provides the finite diagonal-sum formula for square matrices. Specializing entries to a field avoids assuming any unreviewed general ring convention; Einstein notation is just shorthand.
formulations.text: Let K be a field, n≥1, and A=(aᵢⱼ)∈Mₙ(K). The trace of A is tr(A)=∑ᵢ₌₁ⁿ aᵢᵢ ∈ K, the finite sum of diagonal entries.

context: Finite-dimensional real affine geometry: subsets of R^d, integer d≥1, with empty hull allowed

formulations.mathematical_rationale: The real coefficient-sum-one requirement is essential and differs from convex combinations, which require nonnegative coefficients; allowing arbitrary finite k but k≥1 makes the empty-set case exactly ∅.
formulations.text: For an integer d≥1 and a set S⊆ℝ^d, aff(S) is the set of all vectors ∑_{i=1}^{k} αᵢxᵢ with k≥1, xᵢ∈S, αᵢ∈ℝ and ∑_{i=1}^{k} αᵢ=1. In particular aff(∅)=∅.

formulations.mathematical_rationale: The intersection characterization is source-backed and equivalent to the finite-combination characterization, explicitly allowing the empty affine-closed set so aff(∅)=∅ without a nonempty affine-subspace convention conflict.
formulations.text: Let d≥1 and S⊆ℝ^d. Define aff(S) as the intersection of all affine-closed subsets C⊆ℝ^d containing S, where affine-closed means containing every finite affine combination of its members; the empty set is affine-closed.

context: Probability theory: two measurable events in a probability space, including probability-zero cases

formulations.mathematical_rationale: The source's unconditional product identity, interpreted via the general independent-family definition, remains valid for P(A)=0 or P(B)=0; conditional-probability formulations need separate nonzero-denominator hypotheses.
formulations.text: For measurable A,B in a probability space (Ω,Σ,P), the events A and B are independent if and only if P(A∩B)=P(A)P(B). No positive-probability assumption is required for this product-rule definition.

context: Probability theory: joint independence of an arbitrary indexed family of measurable events

formulations.mathematical_rationale: Every finite index subset is required, not merely every size-two subset; under the empty-index convention both sides equal 1, and repeated equal events at different indices still count as distinct indexed entries.
formulations.text: For a probability space (Ω,Σ,P) and indexed measurable events (Aᵢ)_{i∈I}, the family is mutually independent if for every finite J⊆I, P(⋂_{j∈J} Aⱼ)=∏_{j∈J}P(Aⱼ), with the empty intersection Ω and empty product 1.

context: Probability theory: pairwise but not necessarily jointly independent indexed measurable events

formulations.mathematical_rationale: Distinct indices are required, because allowing i=j forces P(Aᵢ)=P(Aᵢ)² and wrongly excludes nontrivial event probabilities; ProofWiki's cardinality-two restatement supports the distinct-index reading despite a displayed quantifier omission.
formulations.text: Let (Aᵢ)_{i∈I} be measurable events on one probability space. The family is pairwise independent if for every i,j∈I with i≠j, P(Aᵢ∩Aⱼ)=P(Aᵢ)P(Aⱼ). This does not in general imply joint independence for three or more events.

context: Graph theory: a finite cycle in a loopless simple undirected graph; length at least three
display_term: cycle in a simple undirected graph

formulations.mathematical_rationale: The source's circuit-with-no-repeated-intermediate-vertex definition specializes to simple undirected loopless graphs; k≥3 excludes loops and length-two parallel-edge cycles allowed by broader multigraph conventions.
formulations.text: For a simple loopless undirected graph G=(V,E), a cycle is a finite cyclic sequence v₀,v₁,…,v_{k−1},v₀ with k≥3, the vertices v₀,…,v_{k−1} pairwise distinct, and {vᵢ,v_{(i+1) mod k}}∈E for every 0≤i<k.

context: Measure theory: extended nonnegative outer measure on the full power set of an arbitrary set X

formulations.mathematical_rationale: Keep empty-set normalization, inclusion monotonicity and countable subadditivity as distinct axioms. The full power-set convention supports arbitrary X including X empty; it is a restricted version of the possible hereditary-sigma-ring domain.
formulations.text: Let X be a set. A function μ*:𝒫(X)→[0,+∞] is an outer measure on X when μ*(∅)=0, A⊆B implies μ*(A)≤μ*(B), and μ*(⋃_{n=1}^∞ Aₙ)≤∑_{n=1}^∞ μ*(Aₙ) for every sequence (Aₙ) of subsets of X.

context: Measure theory on a nonempty metric space (X,d): metric additivity strengthening of a full-power-set outer measure

formulations.mathematical_rationale: The Encyclopedia of Mathematics Definition 3 imposes exact additivity on positively separated subsets. We separately require the standard monotone outer-measure axioms; nonempty X matches the existing independently sourced metric-space meaning and inf-empty convention handles empty A or B.
formulations.text: Let (X,d) be a nonempty metric space and let μ*:𝒫(X)→[0,+∞] be an outer measure. It is a metric outer measure if μ*(A∪B)=μ*(A)+μ*(B) whenever A,B⊆X and inf{d(a,b):a∈A,b∈B}>0, taking inf∅=+∞ when one set is empty.

context: Point-set topology: connectedness of any topological space, including the empty space

formulations.mathematical_rationale: The no-separation characterization is direct from ProofWiki; empty X counts connected because there is no partition into nonempty open subsets, and no Hausdorff or other separation axiom is imposed.
formulations.text: A topological space (X,τ) is connected if there do not exist U,V∈τ with U≠∅, V≠∅, U∩V=∅ and U∪V=X.

formulations.mathematical_rationale: ProofWiki states and proves equivalence of the clopen-set characterization and absence of an open separation. The formulation includes the empty ambient space and requires only the open-set topology.
formulations.text: A topological space (X,τ) is connected if every subset C⊆X that is both open and closed in X satisfies C=∅ or C=X.

context: Abstract algebra: left action of a group G on an arbitrary set X

formulations.mathematical_rationale: Both identity and compatibility are required; order matters in a nonabelian group. Explicit domain G×X distinguishes this left action from a right action, and X may be empty without contradiction.
formulations.text: Let (G,·) be a group with identity e and let X be a set. A left action is a map α:G×X→X such that α(e,x)=x and α(g,α(h,x))=α(g·h,x) for all g,h∈G and x∈X.

context: Abstract algebra: right action of a group G on an arbitrary set X

formulations.mathematical_rationale: The source-specific ordered composition β(β(x,g),h)=β(x,gh) is required; reversing the group multiplication would change the right-action convention. The domain X×G and identity law distinguish it from a left action; empty X allowed.
formulations.text: Let (G,·) be a group with identity e and let X be a set. A right action is a map β:X×G→X such that β(x,e)=x and β(β(x,g),h)=β(x,g·h) for all g,h∈G and x∈X.

context: Functional analysis: linear map X→Y between real or complex normed spaces with one global bound

formulations.mathematical_rationale: The uniform quantifier ∃M∀x is essential; ∀x∃M yields a condition automatically true for any linear map and is defective. A common scalar field and specified domain/codomain norms are retained.
formulations.text: Let X,Y be normed vector spaces over the same field F∈{ℝ,ℂ} and T:X→Y a linear map. T is bounded if there exists a real M≥0 such that ||Tx||_Y≤M||x||_X for every x∈X.

context: Functional analysis: operator norm on real/complex bounded linear maps between normed spaces
display_term: norm of a bounded linear transformation

formulations.mathematical_rationale: Uses the source-backed supremum over the unit ball, including x=0. Boundedness ensures a finite supremum and allows X={0}, where ||T||=0.
formulations.text: For a bounded linear T:X→Y between real or complex normed vector spaces, define ||T||=sup{||Tx||_Y : x∈X, ||x||_X≤1}. This is a finite nonnegative real number.

formulations.mathematical_rationale: The alternative infimum-of-uniform-bounds formulation is equivalent to the unit-ball supremum; no illegal norm of Tx in X is used when T maps X into a different Y.
formulations.text: For bounded linear T:X→Y between real or complex normed spaces, equivalently ||T||=inf{M>0 : ||Tx||_Y≤M||x||_X for all x∈X}, with infimum taken in [0,+∞].

context: Graph theory: fixed integer k≥1, loopless simple undirected graph; coloring need not use every palette color

formulations.mathematical_rationale: The source specifies a mapping to a palette with k labels and differing adjacent colors. This is separate from chromatic number (minimum k) and permits unused colors, including for an empty vertex set.
formulations.text: Let G=(V,E) be a loopless simple undirected graph and let k≥1 be an integer. A proper vertex k-coloring of G is a map c:V→{1,…,k} such that for every edge {u,v}∈E, c(u)≠c(v). Surjectivity is not required.

context: Metric spaces: globally Lipschitz mapping with a constant strictly below one

formulations.mathematical_rationale: Contraction is a pointwise global metric inequality, not a fixed-point theorem; no completeness or self-map is assumed. Domain and codomain metric spaces are nonempty to match the existing sourced metric-space meaning.
formulations.text: Let (X,d_X) and (Y,d_Y) be nonempty metric spaces and f:X→Y. The map f is a contraction if there exists q∈[0,1) such that d_Y(f(x),f(y))≤q·d_X(x,y) for all x,y∈X.
